overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how bias enters AI systems and how fairness is judged. You'll be asked about sources of bias, the COMPAS findings and the vendor's reply, competing definitions of fairness, and audits and notice for automated decisions.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A health algorithm was built to find the patients with the greatest medical needs. It gave Black patients lower scores than equally sick white patients, although race was not one of its inputs. What caused this?

options.html: Its builders added a rule that lowered scores for Black patients
options.text: Its builders added a rule that lowered scores for Black patients
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No such rule existed, and the study found no intent. The algorithm predicted health care cost as a stand-in for illness, and less was spent on Black patients.

options.html: It predicted health care cost as a stand-in for illness
options.text: It predicted health care cost as a stand-in for illness
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Because of unequal access to care, less money was spent on Black patients than on equally sick white patients, so a cost prediction understated their needs.

options.html: It was trained on records that left out most Black patients
options.text: It was trained on records that left out most Black patients
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The problem wasn't missing patients. The algorithm predicted health care cost as a stand-in for illness, and less was spent on Black patients.

options.html: It made inaccurate predictions about what patients would cost
options.text: It made inaccurate predictions about what patients would cost
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Its cost predictions were accurate. The bias arose because it predicted health care cost as a stand-in for illness, and less was spent on Black patients.

forms.stemHtml: ProPublica's analysis of the COMPAS risk score found a difference between Black and white defendants. What was it?

options.html: Black defendants were given a different questionnaire from white defendants
options.text: Black defendants were given a different questionnaire from white defendants
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The questionnaire was the same and didn't ask about race. Among people who didn't reoffend, Black defendants were labeled higher risk nearly twice as often.

options.html: The same score predicted very different reoffending rates for each group
options.text: The same score predicted very different reoffending rates for each group
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A given score meant much the same for both groups, which was the vendor's defense. ProPublica found that among people who didn't reoffend, Black defendants were labeled higher risk nearly twice as often.

options.html: White defendants were scored by judges and Black defendants by software
options.text: White defendants were scored by judges and Black defendants by software
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. All defendants were scored by the same software. Among people who didn't reoffend, Black defendants were labeled higher risk nearly twice as often.

options.html: Black defendants who didn't reoffend were more often labeled higher risk
options.text: Black defendants who didn't reoffend were more often labeled higher risk
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Among defendants who didn't reoffend, 44.9 percent of Black defendants and 23.5 percent of white defendants had been labeled higher risk.

forms.stemHtml: The company that sold COMPAS defended it by saying the score was calibrated. What does that mean?

options.html: A given score matched the same real reoffending rate in both groups
options.text: A given score matched the same real reoffending rate in both groups
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Calibration is the property that a given score corresponds to the same real rate of the outcome in every group.

options.html: Equal numbers of Black and white defendants were labeled higher risk
options.text: Equal numbers of Black and white defendants were labeled higher risk
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Calibration isn't about equal numbers. It means a given score matched the same real reoffending rate in both groups.

options.html: The score had been checked and approved by an independent auditor
options.text: The score had been checked and approved by an independent auditor
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Calibration is a property of the scores, not an approval. It means a given score matched the same real reoffending rate in both groups.

options.html: The score's errors were divided equally between the two groups
options.text: The score's errors were divided equally between the two groups
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That describes error-rate balance, which COMPAS didn't meet. Calibration means a given score matched the same real reoffending rate in both groups.

forms.stemHtml: A 2016 proof showed that three reasonable fairness conditions for a risk score can't all hold except in special cases. What follows from this?

options.html: Bias in automated systems can't be reduced by any method
options.text: Bias in automated systems can't be reduced by any method
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Fixing skewed data or a poor proxy can improve a system on every measure. The proof shows that choosing among fairness conditions is a value choice.

options.html: Calibration is the mathematically correct definition of fairness
options.text: Calibration is the mathematically correct definition of fairness
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The proof shows that the conditions conflict and doesn't rank them. Choosing among them is a value choice.

options.html: Choosing among fairness conditions is a value choice
options.text: Choosing among fairness conditions is a value choice
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! When base rates differ and prediction is imperfect, at least one condition must fail. Mathematics shows the conflict and doesn't say which condition matters more.

options.html: Every automated system is exactly as unfair as every other
options.text: Every automated system is exactly as unfair as every other
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Systems can differ widely in how far they depart from each condition. The proof shows that choosing among fairness conditions is a value choice.

forms.stemHtml: Which statements about bias audits of automated hiring tools are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: An audit compares a tool's outcomes across groups
options.text: An audit compares a tool's outcomes across groups
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A bias audit tests whether a system's outcomes differ across groups, such as by sex or race.

options.html: An audit can miss groups it wasn't set up to test for
options.text: An audit can miss groups it wasn't set up to test for
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! An audit by sex and race won't detect a disadvantage by age, disability, or dialect.

options.html: A tool that passes an audit is fair by every definition
options.text: A tool that passes an audit is fair by every definition
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. An audit tests one measure, and a tool can pass on that measure and fail on another.

options.html: New York City requires an audit, public results, and notice to candidates
options.text: New York City requires an audit, public results, and notice to candidates
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The city prohibits use of an automated employment decision tool unless it has had a bias audit within a year, information about the audit is public, and candidates have been given notice.

title: Bias, fairness, and automated decisions
